definitions.explanation: A social class designation established in the early Meiji era for families of former samurai. After the abolition of the feudal class system, samurai families were officially reclassified as shizoku, a status that was maintained in family registers until 1947.

examples.japanese: {明治|めいじ}{維新|いしん}で{武士|ぶし}は{士族|しぞく}となった。
examples.english: With the Meiji Restoration, samurai became shizoku.

examples.japanese: {士族|しぞく}の{反乱|はんらん}が{各地|かくち}で{起|お}きた。
examples.english: Shizoku rebellions broke out across the country.

examples.japanese: {特権|とっけん}を{失|うしな}った{士族|しぞく}の{多|おお}くは{経済的|けいざいてき}に{困窮|こんきゅう}し、{新|あたら}しい{職業|しょくぎょう}を{探|さが}さなければならなかった。
examples.english: Many shizoku who lost their privileges fell into economic hardship and had to find new occupations.

notes:
USAGE:
A historical term from the Meiji period (1868–1912). The Meiji government abolished the feudal class system and reclassified the population as {華族|かぞく} (peerage/former nobility), {士族|しぞく} (former samurai), and {平民|へいみん} (commoners).

The expression {士族|しぞく}の{商法|しょうほう} (a samurai's way of doing business) is an idiom describing amateurish business practices by former samurai who had no experience with commerce.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {士族|しぞく}の{反乱|はんらん}: shizoku rebellion
- {士族|しぞく}の{商法|しょうほう}: amateurish business (idiom)
- {士族|しぞく}{授産|じゅさん}: relief programs for former samurai
